item.title: The morning after: A question of accountability. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bad things happen everywhere. That is the human condition, not a national indictment.
On the same day in late August that a family of four was killed in Bangladesh, a seventeen-year-old schoolgirl was stabbed to death in Sweden, and in Britain several young men died in a car crash during a police pursuit.
No society, however ordered, is spared sudden and terrible loss.
The measure of a state, then, is never whether tragedy occurs. It is what the state does the morning after.
In Sweden and in Britain, elected governments set the machinery of justice in motion -- investigation, disclosure, prosecution, public accounting. Bangladesh also has an elected government. Yet here the machinery too often produces an explanation faster than it produces evidence.
That is the difference that should concern every citizen. And minorities are simply where that difference becomes visible first.
Consider the case that prompts this. Ganapati Chakraborty spent his working life in a classroom. He taught at Rangpur Zilla School until his retirement last year, and by the accounts of his former students, he was the kind of teacher a town remembers.
On the night of August 20, in the Machuapara neighbourhood of Rangpur, he was killed in his own house, along with his wife Pritilata, their daughter, and their young son. The bodies were found two days later.
Two young men were arrested quickly and gave confessional statements before a magistrate. Since then, the police account of what happened inside that house has changed on more than one occasion, and the relatives of the dead have publicly disputed it.
On August 26, community organizations stood in a human chain before the National Press Club in Dhaka and asked for one thing: A judicial investigation, so that whatever the truth is, it may be established rather than announced.
Days later, in Chandpur, a businessman named Pintu Das disappeared together with his wife and their two sons. Relatives say he had been threatened. The police say they are looking into it.
Who killed the Chakraborty family is not known. What has become of the Das family is not known. Neither, at this moment, does the country -- and that is the point.
When the killing of a schoolteacher’s entire household produces an explanation faster than it produces evidence, something larger than one case is lost. What is lost is the public’s belief that the state is able to find out the truth at all.
What is happening is not sudden
It would be convenient to treat the Rangpur killings as an aberration, a crime like any other. The longer record makes that difficult.
Professor Abul Barkat of Dhaka University spent three decades studying what the Enemy Property Act and its successor, the Vested Property Act, did to this country’s Hindu citizens.
His finding was not about riots; it was about paperwork. Roughly 2.6 million acres were taken from Hindu families, and around 60% of Bangladesh’s Hindus were left landless.
In 2005 the United States State Department put the figure at about 2.5 million acres and estimated that nearly every Hindu family in the country had been touched by it.
The Vested Property Return Act was amended in 2011, largely because of the movement that Professor Barkat’s work helped to build. Restitution has still barely happened.
The census tells the second half of the story. In 1951, Hindus were a little over a fifth of the population. In 1974, 13.5%. In 2011, 8.54%. In 2022, 7.95%.
The absolute number has held roughly steady at 13 million, so this is not a community disappearing overnight. It is something slower and, in a way, sadder: A community that does not grow, because in every generation a portion of it quietly concludes there is no future here and leaves.
Professor Barkat gave this process a precise name. He called it unpeopling -- not the sudden violence that makes the newspapers, but the steady administrative and social pressure that makes staying unreasonable.
No government of Bangladesh invented this. Every government since 1971 has inherited it, and none has ended it. But it can only end under a government that decides to end it.
Beyond Minneapolis
Some years ago I wrote publicly, more than once, about the killing of George Floyd, as millions did who had never been to Minneapolis and had no personal stake in it.
I supported the movement that gathered under the words Black Lives Matter, and said so in letters to The New York Times. My sadness was such that I proposed, in one of them, that Washington Avenue be renamed George Floyd Avenue -- a small gesture of moral protest from very far away.
I want to be careful about why that case mattered, because the principle travels and the slogan is often misheard.
The principle behind those three words was never that only some lives matter. It was the opposite: That a life reliably ignored is the emergency -- that when a whole category of deaths dependably produces no consequence, the problem is not the individual death but the system around it.
The demand that followed was startlingly modest: Count the deaths honestly, investigate them as you would any other, and prosecute without regard to who the dead man was.
That principle has no borders and belongs to no one community. It can be applied in Bangladesh without importing a single foreign idea, because it is already written into our own constitution.
A country in which some citizens’ deaths are investigated seriously and others’ are explained away is not a country with a minority problem. It is a country with a rule-of-law problem -- and the minority is simply where that problem becomes visible first.
What should be done
The remedies are small, and each is within the government’s power.
Order a judicial investigation into the Rangpur killings, and let it go wherever the evidence goes. Find the Das family. Try these cases in open court, publish the verdicts, and accept the outcome even when it is inconvenient.
Instruct the police that a confession is where an investigation begins and not where it ends, and discipline officers who close files rather than solve them. Resume the return of vested property, which is 15 years overdue.
And let the state itself collect and publish honest national data on communal violence -- because at present the only figures available come from advocacy organizations, and a government that disputes those figures has an obvious remedy: Publish better ones.
Let me also say plainly what I am not saying, because in this country such things are heard before they are read.
I am not saying that the Muslims of Bangladesh are the enemies of the Hindus of Bangladesh. In every bad season we have had, including this one, it has been Muslim neighbours who sheltered Hindu families. I am not calling for retaliation of any kind; anyone who answers murder with murder has become the thing he feared.
And I am not inviting any foreign government to adopt this community as an instrument of its own quarrels. Minorities who become another country’s talking point end up less safe, not more. This is a Bangladeshi matter, to be settled in Bangladeshi courts.
Nor is this a Hindu matter alone. Impunity has no religion and no loyalty. The same police stations and the same courts that fail a Hindu family in Rangpur are failing Muslim families elsewhere, and the political killings that were promised to end have not ended.
Minorities are only where the failure shows itself first, because we have the least protection and the fewest voices raised on our behalf. We are the early warning. We are not the exception.
This is not, in the end, a plea for the protection of Hindus. It is a plea for the ordinary functioning of a state that means what it says.
Rajani K Saha writes from Sweden and is a practising physician.

item.title: Saving the Sundarbans from criminality. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The reopening of the Sundarbans is welcome news for thousands of fishermen, forest workers, and others whose livelihoods depend on the forest. It is unfortunate to note, thus, that piracy has once again become a serious threat in the area.
While many finally have an opportunity to return to work after three months of closure, and begin recovering from the financial strain that has accumulated in their absence, returning to the forest also means returning to fear.
Fishermen have reported being forced to pay extortion money to criminal groups in exchange for so-called tokens or slips that supposedly allow them to enter particular parts of the forest safely. Those who refuse can face abduction, assault and ransom demands.
For some locals, the threat from pirates has become more frightening than the forest's natural dangers.
This is unacceptable; people should not have to choose between risking their lives and abandoning their livelihoods.
These communities already live with poverty, debt, and the uncertainties of climate and nature. The return of organized criminal groups should not add another burden to their lives.
There have been encouraging efforts: Recent Coast Guard operations have resulted in arrests, weapons seizures, and the rescue of hostages, while several groups and their members have surrendered.
But sporadic successes cannot substitute for sustained security. Authorities must intensify coordinated patrols, intelligence gathering, and surveillance throughout the forest and its waterways.
Law enforcement agencies must also establish reliable channels through which fishermen can report threats without fearing retaliation.
Most importantly, those who finance, organize, and participate in these criminal networks must face justice.
The Sundarbans belongs to the nation, but its protection is inseparable from protecting the people who depend on it. A forest cannot truly be considered secure when the communities entering it for their livelihoods remain unsafe.
Making the Sundarbans safe for all who depend on it must be treated as a priority.

item.title: Matching environmental responsibility at home. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As a country that contributes comparatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions yet remains highly vulnerable to climate change, Bangladesh's demands for greater climate finance, adaptation support, and accountability from major emitters are both justified and necessary.
Yet despite being among the strongest voices for climate justice on the international stage, the latest Environmental Performance Index (EPI) offers an uncomfortable reminder: Climate leadership abroad must be matched by environmental responsibility at home.
Bangladesh ranks 175th out of 177 countries in the EPI 2026, with a score of 23.46 out of 100, and a particularly poor performance in air quality and ecosystem vitality.
Our rivers continue to suffer from industrial waste, sewage, plastic, and encroachment. Wetlands are disappearing under unplanned urbanization, while Dhaka's air remains dangerously polluted by vehicle emissions, construction dust, and other sources.
These are environmental concerns that directly affect public health, livelihoods, productivity, and the quality of life of millions.
Most concerning, however, is that Bangladesh does not necessarily lack policies or laws. The greater problem is implementation. Environmental regulations mean little when industries can evade pollution controls, wetlands can be filled, rivers can be occupied, and waste can be dumped with limited consequences.
Stronger enforcement, institutional coordination, and accountability are therefore essential.
This should also be viewed as an issue of climate justice: The right to clean air, safe water, and a healthy environment cannot be separated from the climate justice Bangladesh advocates for internationally. Protecting vulnerable communities and restoring damaged ecosystems must become central to national development.
Ultimately, we should continue demanding greater responsibility from the international community, but we must also demonstrate that responsibility ourselves.
Bangladesh's credibility as a climate champion will depend not only on what it says at global conferences, but on whether its citizens can also see and breathe the difference at home.

item.title: The reality of revolutions. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Facilitating the legacy of civil movements is challenging for both organizers and the public trying to change established autocratic governments. One major challenge after such movements is gaining trust and support for the new political system among citizens and various groups, both locally and internationally.
To address this, it is essential to build legitimacy, create effective government structures, and develop a sense of ownership among the people. It is also important to engage with international organizations to get recognition and support for the transition process.
The main structural issue is the struggle for power and leadership that follows an autocratic regime's collapse. When a former government falls apart, it creates a power vacuum. This can cause different revolutionary groups to split and compete with one another, leading to ideological fragmentation within the movement spirit.
The worrying factor is that without unity, there may be internal conflicts or a worrying shift back to authoritarian rule, both of which run counter to the movement's short- and long-term goals.
Karl Marx posited that revolutions arise from the intrinsic contradictions and conflicts embedded within class structures, particularly the antagonism between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. As socio-economic inequalities intensify, the disenfranchised class mobilizes to dismantle the existing capitalist framework and establish a new socio-political paradigm.
Marx, in addition, argued that the inherent conflicts between social classes, notably between capitalists and workers, and the ensuing struggles for power, are fundamentally rooted in the unequal distribution of wealth and resources. This dynamic sets the stage for class consciousness to develop, ultimately driving revolutionary change in response to systemic oppression to avoid alienation from society.
Vladimir Lenin's Vanguard theory can also be understood in relation to the classification between movement and revolution. He stressed the importance of an organized group of revolutionaries to lead the working class in achieving socialism.
Although the July-August 2024 movement in Bangladesh did not reflect the spirit of the socialist movement, these theories played out during the expected 2024 upsurge, highlighting the relationship between organized movements and the public. It could offer insights into how effective a vanguard can be in gathering support, addressing social and economic problems, and promoting political change in Bangladesh.
Lenin’s Vanguard theory suggests that workers, or in Bangladesh's case, students, needed guidance to develop revolutionary awareness. This highlights the need for a well-disciplined revolutionary political party, which was absent during the movement in Bangladesh and is highly unlikely to emerge in the future.
Crane Brinton stated in “ The Anatomy of Revolution ” that the challenge of establishing a lasting order from the aftermath of a revolution frequently results in internal conflict and ultimately authoritarian rule. In his observation, Brinton likely noted that creating a new, stable system after a revolution can be challenging when the previous one has collapsed.
I have observed that differing perspectives and vested interests among societal factions can significantly complicate the rebuilding of the nation’s socio-economic and socio-political institutions in a spirit of democracy, even though the democratic process does not always yield ultimate success for nation-states.
These divergent views frequently result in conflicts that escalate over time. In such scenarios, it is not uncommon for a singular leader or faction to amass disproportionate power to reestablish order. However, this concentration of authority often compromises individual liberties and undermines the principles of democratic governance.
The lack of institutional capacity poses a significant challenge for states undergoing revolutions aimed at transforming the old autocratic structures. While revolutions can dismantle outdated institutions, they often fail to create stable and inclusive ones. This absence can lead to governance breakdown or a return to centralized control.
An American political sociologist, Barrington Moore Jr (1966), noted that economic pressures from significant changes can alienate supporters and strengthen counter-revolutionary forces. He illustrated this with Venezuela's Bolivarian Revolution under Hugo Chávez, which launched social reforms but collapsed due to economic mismanagement and overreliance on oil.
Additionally, external interference from groups supporting authoritarian governments can weaken revolutions through military action, sanctions, or backing counterrevolutionary movements.
Jack Goldstone, an American sociologist, political scientist, and historian, in his (2001) piece, critically analyzed revolution and rebellion in the early modern world. He argued that revolutionary governments encounter significant external opposition, which constrains their independence and chances of survival.
The Cuban Revolution endured largely due to Soviet support despite US efforts to undermine it, like the Bay of Pigs invasion and the embargo. Following revolutions often lead to revolutionary fatigue and disillusionment with ideals such as equality and justice, as ongoing instability wears on citizens. Hannah Arendt noted that the initial fervor often gives way to disappointment over unmet commitments.
The Iranian Revolution (1979), which began with anti-authoritarian goals, eventually resulted in a theocratic regime with authoritarian governance, raising questions about Iranians' collective perception of its outcome. Counter-revolutionary forces, such as displaced elites and military bodies, frequently resist and can reclaim power.
In the book Age of Extremes , the British historian Eric Hobsbawm (1994) argues that successful revolutions are uncommon because old ruling classes and their deep-rooted stakeholders, both domestically and externally, usually possess the means to hinder change. For instance, during the French Revolution, monarchist forces continually weakened the movement, leading to Napoleon's rise to power.
Why have numerous strong revolutions not been sustained in Bangladesh ?
Since the nation's liberation, examining post-revolution power struggles and authoritarianism is foundational to understanding the lack of a sustainable revolution in an independent Bangladesh.
After the 1971 Liberation War, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's leadership aimed to create a new state. However, internal divisions, economic issues, and political opposition led to a one-party rule (BAKSAL) in 1975, followed by substantial military rule until 1990.
Rounaq Jahan (2005) argued in her piece: "Bangladesh: Promise and Performance" that authoritarianism and elite conflicts hindered the establishment of democracy, resulting in coups and instability.
While military regimes framed themselves as stabilizers, their use of revolutionary rhetoric without implementing necessary reforms was unpopular among the state's citizens.
Fragile political institutions prioritize control over governance, leading to poor governance and disrupted citizen well-being. Strong institutions are essential for sustainable governance, but in Bangladesh, partisan politics, corruption, and patronage systems have consistently undermined this development.
Clear objectives allowed key movements in East Pakistan to gain recognition among the majority population. The Language Movement in 1952 aimed to establish “Bangla” as an official language, while the 1971 Liberation War sought self-determination against West Pakistani dominance. Badruddin Umar (2004) in “ The Emergence of Bangladesh ” identifies the Language Movement as a pivotal moment for Bengali nationalism, emphasizing the importance of cultural identity in fueling collective action.
Ahmed Rafiuddin's (2004) work, “ The Bengal Muslims, 1871–1906 ”, highlights how clear goals and national identity underpinned successful revolutionary movements in Bangladesh, leading to widespread support across social classes. In contrast to unsuccessful revolutions elsewhere, these movements involved students, workers, peasants, professionals, and civil servants.
Bose Sarmila (2011) in “ Dead Reckoning: Memories of the 1971 Bangladesh War ” describes the 1971 war as a social revolution, involving diverse participants across religions and classes, characterized by an inclusive and nationalistic spirit.
Effective leaders in revolutionary movements demonstrate significant charisma and actively engage with grassroots constituents, effectively aligning popular movements with specific political objectives.
This dynamic was exemplified by the Six-Point Movement of 1966 in East Pakistan, where nationalist leaders adeptly transformed cultural grievances into a coherent secessionist strategy. This approach channeled widespread public discontent into organized action, thereby mitigating potential chaos.
The oppressive policies enacted by West Pakistan, characterized by economic inequity and military repression, created a moral impetus for revolution. The violent crackdown known as Operation Searchlight in 1971 intensified calls for independence, fortifying internal solidarity while simultaneously garnering international support.
International backing proved critical to the success of the 1971 Bangladesh independence movement. It played a pivotal role in shaping military dynamics, securing diplomatic recognition, and amplifying humanitarian awareness.
While the primary driving force behind the movement was the local populace and the Mukti Bahini, external support was instrumental in facilitating the eventual liberation of Bangladesh.
In a parallel instance, the mass mobilization that occurred in 1990 culminated in the ousting of Hussain Muhammad Ershad’s military regime. This movement, propelled by extensive public engagement and international pressure, marked a significant transition from dictatorship to parliamentary democracy in Bangladesh.
The July-August movement in Bangladesh was underpinned by a sustained wave of mass protests against the autocratic regime that had been ongoing since 2009. This mobilization culminated in pivotal events on August 5, 2024, highlighting a significant coalition of support from both the elite and general populace.
This scenario illustrates a practical application of Lenin's theory on the necessity of mass participation and leadership to facilitate revolutionary change; the experience in Bangladesh demonstrates that without widespread engagement and strategic direction, achieving governmental control can prove exceptionally challenging.
Has the recent movement failed in Bangladesh?
To understand the challenges faced by movements in Bangladesh, it is essential to look beyond street demonstrations. While many mass movements gain momentum, they often struggle to effect lasting change due to structural, political, and social barriers.
Since Bangladesh's independence in 1971, efforts have been hampered by a lack of a unified ideology, societal fragmentation among political parties, internal divisions, weak institutions, economic disruptions, external opposition, and declining revolutionary ideals, all of which hinder the sustainability of post-revolutionary governance. Most importantly, movements or revolutions have failed due to:
(a) elites and vested interested groups’ manipulation in the process of transferring basic structural reforms within the state’s social, political and legal institutions;
(b) authoritarian reactions;
(c) internal divisions within the movement organizers and followers.
To achieve enduring change, movements require ongoing civic involvement, institutional partnerships, and a distinct vision for democracy, not merely the ousting of specific leaders or regimes.
Many movements are reactionary, focusing on removing leaders or achieving electoral victory without clear plans to reform institutions such as the judiciary or the police. These movements often lack institutional grounding, allowing the old system to revive once initial enthusiasm fades.
In Bangladesh, political parties frequently appropriate grassroots movements to enhance their electoral prospects, only to perpetuate corrupt practices once in office. This dynamic engenders a significant disconnect, wherein grassroots activists perceive themselves as marginalized, as political leaders exploit public discontent for their personal or factional agendas
In my assessment, drawing upon extensive longitudinal observations of Bangladeshi society, the pathway to sustainable transformation in Bangladesh necessitates a cultural revolution that fundamentally reconfigures societal values, norms, and institutional frameworks.
Unlike political revolutions that primarily alter governing bodies, cultural revolutions aim to modify the foundational societal constructs, thereby impacting domains such as education, the arts, and social interactions. The primary attributes of this transformative process include:
(a) Ideological shift to change national beliefs;
(b) Public mobilization for norm transformation;
(c) Repression of old values through censorship;
(d) State or movement-driven initiatives;
(e) Enduring effects on institutions like education and family.
Preserving the momentum and legacy of a mass movement is a complex but essential task. Following the July-August 2024 movement in Bangladesh, one of the most important challenges has been transforming public aspirations into sustainable democratic and institutional reforms.
Achieving this requires building citizens' confidence, strengthening public institutions, and fostering trust among domestic and international stakeholders. While significant opportunities have emerged, the long-term success of the movement will depend on the ability of political and social actors to work collaboratively toward inclusive governance and national development.
Bangladesh has the potential to improve its chances of sustaining a revolution or upsurge that truly changes society and governance by nurturing a cultural revolution. This would also create an atmosphere conducive to the flourishing of democratic ideals and a just society.
Dr ASM Anam Ullah (PhD) is an Australian senior academic, editor, human rights activist, political analyst, and OHS and industrial relations expert.

item.title: Reassess the economics of the Bay Terminal. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is aspiring to become a trillion-dollar economy, an export powerhouse, and a future regional manufacturing hub. Given these ambitions, investing in world-class ports sounds like an obvious step.
But successful nations are rarely defined by how much infrastructure they build. Instead, they are defined by the discipline they bring to the decision making around what to build, when to build it, and at what cost.
That is precisely why the Bay Terminal deserves a fresh, evidence-based reassessment.
If Bangladesh can unlock substantially more capacity from the ports it already has, shouldn't we wring out those gains before committing billions more to another mega-project while our purchasing power is already strained?
That question is no longer theoretical. In 2025, Chittagong Port Authority handled a record 3.409 million TEUs of containers -- including roughly 750,000 empty boxes -- while carrying 92% of Bangladesh's international trade and nearly 98% of its containerized cargo.
For an economy this size, a port carrying that much of the national trade load is not merely infrastructure. It is the country's economic heartbeat.
Yet beneath the headlines about new megaprojects sits a less-told story. Operational assessments suggest that simply modernizing what already exists -- the New Mooring Container Terminal, the Chittagong Container Terminal, the general cargo berths, and a fully utilized Patenga Container Terminal -- could lift annual handling capacity from roughly 34 lakh TEUs to about 46 lakh TEUs according to a study.
That is a nearly 35% increase without building a single new deep-sea terminal -- on its own, roughly equivalent to adding the throughput of a mid-sized port.
The picture becomes more compelling still. Matarbari Deep Sea Port is already under construction, and the completion of its first phase is projected to lift Bangladesh's total container handling capacity to approximately 54 lakh TEUs -- almost a 60% increase over current throughput. Add APM Terminals' new facility and Matarbari's second phase, and overall national capacity could reach around 88 lakh TEUs -- roughly 2.6 times what the country handles today.
These numbers invite an obvious policy question: Should Bangladesh first optimize, modernize, and fully use the capacity it already has -- and the capacity already nearing completion -- before committing to another capital-intensive port expansion?
This is not an argument against development. It is an argument for sequencing it well.
Singapore continuously modernizes its existing terminals while sequencing expansion decades in advance. The Port of Rotterdam invests as heavily in automation, hinterland connectivity, and logistics integration as it does in physical infrastructure.
Busan's competitive edge comes as much from operational productivity as from additional berths. In global port economics, capacity is one variable, productivity is the multiplier.
That distinction matters because of opportunity costs. Bangladesh remains a capital-constrained economy, and every additional billion dollars committed to one project is a billion dollars unavailable for energy security, rail connectivity, inland logistics, climate resilience, education, or healthcare.
Infrastructure planning, in that sense, is an exercise in capital allocation as much as engineering.
This is where the Bay Terminal deserves closer scrutiny. Accommodating larger, deep-draft vessels will require substantial capital dredging, along with recurring maintenance dredging over the life of the project.
One estimate places initial dredging costs at$150-160 million, with annual maintenance potentially reaching $20-25m -- though these figures need independent engineering validation.
For scale, the World Bank has already approved a $650m loan to help finance the breakwater and access-channel dredging alone, a reminder that headline dredging estimates for the project tend to be a floor rather than a ceiling.
These costs are not, by themselves, reasons to abandon the project. They are reasons to make sure every assumption behind it is rigorously tested.
Bangladesh has already learned this lesson once, at Payra. That port's experience shows how sediment dynamics, navigation constraints, and long-term dredging needs can significantly affect operational economics over time.
Bay Terminal is a different project with different engineering characteristics, and the two should not be treated as identical. But Payra is a reminder that a port's success is measured not by its ribbon-cutting ceremony, but by its ability to operate efficiently, sustainably, and economically over the following 30 years.
Encouragingly, reports indicate that the Bay Terminal feasibility assessment is being revisited. That should be welcomed. It is an opportunity to do something Bangladesh has rarely attempted: A comprehensive national port optimization strategy.
Rather than evaluating Bay Terminal in isolation, policy-makers should weigh it against every realistic alternative such as modernizing NCT and CCT, fully utilising Patenga, accelerating Matarbari, improving rail and inland container logistics, expanding automation, and widening private-sector participation.
Only then can the country work out which sequence of investments delivers the highest economic return per taka spent.
The debate, then, is not whether Bangladesh needs the Bay Terminal. It is whether the Bay Terminal should be the next investment or whether smarter, faster, and more cost-effective options can deliver the same economic benefits while preserving scarce public resources.
Nations rarely grow prosperous because they build the biggest infrastructure. They grow prosperous because they build the right infrastructure, at the right time, in the right sequence, with the discipline to question even their most ambitious ideas.
As Bangladesh charts its maritime future, that discipline may prove to be the most valuable investment decision of all.
Ashfaq Zaman is the founder of Dhaka Forum and a strategic international affairs expert.

item.title: Playing Russian roulette with Pakistani rain. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Sulaiman, a school teacher in Buner, lives in a pocket of Pakistan hemmed in between Mardan, Swat and Swabi, where life is village and mountain stream and the fame of a valley charming and fertile. Climate ruin was an affliction reserved for places with mighty rivers such as the Swat or the Kunar. It made sense because Buner had none of these. Just sweet little springs trickling softly through the rocks.

That perception was pulverised on August 15, 2025.

It began as the sort of unassuming Friday that tricks you into believing you have the upper hand on the day. At 8:30 AM, Sulaiman could hear the rain tapping on the roof as he buttoned his shalwar kameez, one of the finer sets reserved for Jummah, before heading out. Within an hour, however, Nature lost its temper and dumped a cloudburst into the mountain-ringed basin.

From the classroom window, he saw a clear ribbon of a stream change into a slurry of liquefied soil. The brown tide smothered houses and shops, sucking cars, trucks, fleeing villagers and everything within the line of sight into its soup. Sulaiman hurriedly dialled his brother at their 33-room ancestral home where the entire family lived. The phone was picked up at the third ring, but before a word could be exchanged, the line went dead.

That day, out of 27 members of his family, 24 had died. An entire lineage and a collective loss estimated at over Rs 210 million were wiped out in the time it took Sulaiman to teach a single class. The survivors waded into the debris to pull bodies from the mud before any help arrived. It took over a week to find the last one.

What incenses Sulaiman the most is the divide between Pakistan’s urban centres and its margins. “We weren’t even asking for a day’s notice,” he says. “If we had received a single alert just 30 minutes before the cloudburst, we could have run up the mountain slopes and taken shelter at the higher houses.” So many lives could have been saved.

Nearly a year later, charities have helped rebuild basic shelter but the terrain remains glutted with stone, and the fields of maize and wheat ruined. Children returned to school but burdened by trauma that resurfaces whenever dark storm clouds gather over the peaks.

Headline after headline has been sounding the alarm. Here’s one that did the rounds last month: Nationwide deaths this monsoon cross 100; more rain likely in the country’s upper parts from July 29. While climate change gets most of the blame, the crisis is equally driven by flawed weather forecasting.

Goliath and Davids

As disaster and climate change specialist Fatima Yamin puts it, the problem is not the availability of information or its lack thereof; it is how it is conveyed to Pakistanis across the country. Broadcasting a storm warning on PTV or flooding a federal Twitter (X) handle does little for a villager in Bagrot Valley at 15,000 feet, or a family living in the parts of Jacobabad that are off the grid. “Not everyone has a TV,” she says, recalling the 2022 image of a family stranded in the middle of a roaring Swat river.

“Where are you sending these warnings? If the prediction of a weather event is that severe, it should be sent as text messages in a language the recipients will understand, echoed over local radio stations in native dialects, and posted on roadside addas and bus stops.” The academic posturing needs to be stripped away so citizens know what actually matters: Will water rise in their locality, on their street, outside their front door, in the next hour?

When a meteorological anomaly brews over a region, the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) generates macro-level predictions. These turn into bulletins that navigate a series of channels to take the form of jargon-laden press releases that at times even disaster scientists struggle to translate, let alone a farmer in Sindh.

The story of weather forecasting in Pakistan is one of a state-backed Goliath equipped with global telecommunications networks, satellite feeds, and Doppler radars, against independent Davids armed with online global weather models, social media pages, and an appetite for public engagement.

To forecast, you have to be intimate with the terrain

To understand why our skies are notoriously difficult to predict, it is helpful to know the inner workings of the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) as revealed by two experts: Dr Ghulam Rasul, its former director-general, and Dr Sardar Sarfaraz, a former Chief Meteorologist.

When Pakistan emerged on the map in 1947, it inherited a network of just nine meteorological observatories. Today, the PMD operates over 100 stations dotted across the country’s diverse climatic zones to study three distinct scientific domains: meteorology, hydrology, and seismology.

To capture the sky’s moods, the department deploys a web of instruments. The stations measure air temperature, wind speed and direction, atmospheric pressure, soil temperature across several depths, hourly rainfall, and visual cloud dynamics. The vertical atmospheric profiling is done by helium-filled weather balloons which release radiosondes or battery-powered telemetry devices that transmit atmospheric parameters every 100 meters as they climb into the upper atmosphere until they burst. Japan has funded Doppler radars in Karachi and Islamabad (alongside older but operational units in Lahore and smaller X, S, and C-band radars across the country) that cover 85 per cent of Pakistan’s landmass. Combined with geostationary satellite feeds, polar-orbiting satellite images, and oceanographic buoys tracking sea surface temperatures, these instruments feed volumes of data into numerical weather prediction models run on high-powered computers.

Crucially, as both experts emphasise, PMD belongs to an exclusive global fraternity. Through the World Meteorological Organisation’s Global Telecommunication System, PMD exchanges real-time upper air and surface data with national services in India, Bangladesh, Japan, and beyond. It is a vast, proprietary data pipeline that no independent forecaster can directly tap into.

Despite this formidable technological array, weather predictions, time and again, fail. Sarfaraz explains why. “Atmospheric science, unlike natural science, is a science of probability and uncertainty where 2 plus 2 don’t always make 4. Sometimes the answer is 5, and sometimes 3.”

He points out that the fundamental nature of the atmosphere is non-linear and inherently chaotic. Computerised numerical weather prediction models rely on physical and mathematical assumptions that do not always match the messy realities of nature. For instance, models generally assume a standard atmospheric lapse rate that temperature drops uniformly by 6 degree celsius per kilometer as you go up. In reality, the upward profile of the atmosphere is erratic; it can shift by 4 degree celsius one day and over 7 degree celsius the next. When initial parameters are off even slightly, computerised models compound these tiny errors over time.

Moreover, accuracy depends heavily on the forecast horizon. Short-range forecast (24–72 hours) has high precision, with typically 90pc or higher accuracy rate. With medium-range (3–7 days), accuracy begins to degrade as model assumptions warp over time. When it comes to long-range forecasts (15 days to 3 months), it drops significantly, often below 70pc, particularly in Pakistan where complex topography dictates abrupt micro-climatic shifts. Added to this are physical data gaps. While 100 observatories sound impressive, Sarfaraz notes that ideally, an observation data point is needed every 50 kilometers and massive blind spots persist over far-flung regions in the country.

There is an art to forecasting that raw computational horsepower cannot replicate: local terrain knowledge.

Global numerical models produced by European or American agencies often struggle to parse localised regional dynamics. Rasul highlights a classic example: tropical cyclones steaming across the Arabian Sea toward the coast of Sindh. When this happens, Western computer models are quick to predict a direct strike on Karachi. However, seasoned local meteorologists know the terrain dynamics that routinely divert these cyclones eastward toward the Rann of Kutch or Gujarat in India.

“A forecaster coming from Islamabad to Karachi to predict its weather would be confused by the city’s skies, where clouds form daily only to dissolve without rain,” he says. “To forecast a place, you have to be intimate with its terrain.”

Predicting severe weather, such as the formation of Cumulonimbus clouds that trigger hailstorms, lightning, and dangerous aviation downdrafts, requires reading colour-coded Doppler radar echoes alongside rising thermal air currents. This is where institutional memory and human intuition come in and interpret what the computer screens output.

The independent weathermen

The stories behind Pakistan’s leading private forecasters could not be more different from the traditional academic-to-bureaucrat pipeline.

Jawad Memon’s entry into meteorology started 15 years ago as a passion project. All he had in his arsenal was a newly installed Wi-Fi connection at home, an obsession with thunderstorms, and hours of self-guided internet research. Memon began sharing informal predictions on social media. This hobby morphed into Weather Updates PK, a platform whose forecasts are routinely picked up by TV channels today. “When thousands of people are following you and the media is looking at your forecasts so closely, you feel a great sense of responsibility,” he says. Direct feedback from a massive social media following holds his work accountable.

Rather than taking computerised simulations at face value, he rigorously filters model outputs through ground parameters, such as tracking wind farm dynamics to see if dry desert air from Rajasthan will disarm an approaching monsoon system over Sindh. He logs his prediction outcomes to calculate error margins and analyse why a forecast failed, aiming for a self-tracked accuracy rate of 85-90 pc.

Memon relies on earnings from an entirely unrelated livelihood to fund the operations: a small business specialising in CCTV surveillance and security equipment. He funnels the profits into his forecasting work, paying for expensive subscriptions to premium global weather models, including the Global Forecast System, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, and ICON, along with deploying a handful of private weather stations in Karachi.

Junaid Yamin, the CEO of Weatherwalay, also has no formal background in meteorology. He took a corporate and technological route, building a private network of around 400 weather stations across Pakistan. They combine real-time data from these physical stations with high-resolution imagery from the European Weather Satellite (EUMETSAT). Their software pipeline ingests and synthesises 10 international weather models simultaneously, using proprietary machine-learning algorithms to track trend patterns over 10 to 14 day horizons. When an anomaly is detected, the platform translates raw synoptic data into alerts that are sent to mobile apps as push notifications.

Weatherwalay employs dedicated AI/ML software engineers whose sole function is to test prediction accuracy and continuously train machine-learning models against ground-truth data from their nationwide stations.

Us vs Them

Us…

Sarfaraz says that sensationalism often fuels private weather pages. “I have observed that they create a lot of unnecessary hype,” he says. “In Karachi’s case specifically, the climate event is usually not as big as it is exaggerated online. Maybe they’re concerned about the likes and followers on their Facebook pages.”

If an independent forecaster makes a correct call, Sarfaraz argues the credit should go to the global models, not the institutions or individuals themselves. He argues this, saying that independent forecasters rely on freely available global datasets without possessing their own physical observation networks, Doppler radars, or upper-air radiosonde feeds.

Rasul, however, acknowledges that while independent forecasters may lack formal degrees in atmospheric sciences, repeated practice and passion have honed their skills, and they fill a vacuum left by PMD’s communication shortcomings.

He recalls recent discussions with an Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) official, who confessed that private digital giants like AccuWeather and Weather Underground are giving state forecasters a run for their money, compelling the IMD to aggressively upgrade its modeling and delivery mechanisms. There might be something to learn from here.

“In a way, it is a positive sign that private weather forecasters are entering the field and competing with national services,” he says. “Currently, the way PMD simply issues long lists of cities across a province where significant weather events rarely happen is hardly effective forecasting. This needs to improve.”

Them…

The tension between state meteorologists and independent analysts often descends into public turf wars. Private weather firecasters argue that these kinds of standoffs leave the public stranded in a dangerous information vacuum.

Memon says that the solution is not to undermine the state’s formal mandate, but to dismantle the barriers that keep private innovators at arm’s length. He points to international precedents of national meteorological agencies nurturing independent analysts with shared data pipelines and subsidised equipment.

He proposes that the government establish a formal, collaborative umbrella for both worlds. The PMD holds the statutory authority and access to multi-million-dollar Doppler radars, but real-world experience, local monitoring, and agility are what modern forecasting demands. When an institution isolates itself from that partnership, it is the country’s farmers, commuters, and urban residents who bear the cost of an institutional divide.

Yamin frames the challenge not as a lack of talent or infrastructure, but an entrenched culture of running administrative silos. Every department and startup tries to reinvent the wheel rather than leverage existing capabilities across public and private lines. Climate specialist Daniel Cull stressed that climate change is a mammoth crisis that neither the public sector, private enterprise, nor non-profits can tackle alone. The World Meteorological Organisation has long advocated for institutionalised public-private engagement precisely because unpredictable weather requires both deep scientific infrastructure and nimble, tech-driven delivery systems.

Yamin, in PMD’s defence, says that the public and media must recognise that atmospheric science is probabilistic. He suggests that official forecasters must frame predictions accurately, communicating likelihoods instead of absolutes, and updating the public continuously as initial parameters evolve.

But collaboration is only half the battle.

To environmental lawyer Ahmad Rafay Alam, the reality that ordinary Pakistanis suffer the brunt of climate disasters only because information is not given in time is the real tragedy. The data exists. The alerts are sent. The breakdown happens because of downstream governance.

“We knew on Friday, July 24, for example, that it was going to rain on the weekend and that there was going to be urban flooding in Lahore and Gujranwala based on a PMD flood forecasting notification issued at 12:10 PM,” he says. “These are official notifications that go to everyone.”

Alam turns to apps such as Weatherwalay for alerts, though accessing wider geographic data requires a subscription. When assessing cross-border hydrology, he sidesteps official channels entirely. “I sometimes jump on my VPN to monitor flood data on Indian websites, as our transboundary river systems and shared geography mean upstream conditions directly affect our own.”

But a vulnerable farmer or katchi abadi dweller has neither a subscription nor guaranteed electricity. That is precisely why Provincial Disaster Management Authorities and district administrations exist. “The disaster management authorities have published a Multi-Hazard Vulnerability Risk Assessments for every district across the provinces,” says Alam. It maps out every threat, fire, drought, floods, and details exactly which infrastructure will be compromised. It’s all published, it’s all online. “I’ve seen whole volumes of it. So it is not a lack of data,” he says. “It’s a question of how you respond to it and get it into the hands of people who lack the equipment and information to protect themselves.”

Nowhere was this dysfunction more glaring than in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa last year. Monsoonal belts tracked unusually north, unleashing catastrophic flash floods across Swat and the valleys while all five rivers in Punjab swelled simultaneously.

Meanwhile, state departments squabbled.

“Last year there was a fight about what the definition of a flash flood is,” Alam recalls. The PMD argued that these rains didn’t fit the classic technical definition—X volume of water falls in Y amount of time. “This kerfuffle was a bit childish.”

In jagged mountain topography, where evacuating communities across gorges is a race against time, rigid meteorological pedantry costs lives. The PMD shouldn’t get bogged down in textbook legalities; it must issue immediate operational alerts to local administrations that a deadly threat is barrelling their way.

Alam is equally quick to push back against scapegoating the PMD for disasters engineered on the ground. In Swat, the wreckage left behind by raging waters exposed systemic governance failures that no radar system could fix.

There is a law in KP—Rivers Protection Ordinance, 2002—which says it is absolutely prohibited to build anything within 150 feet of the high-water mark of any river. “Now you tell me: what have people been doing on riverbanks for over two decades since that law came in? Building continuously,” says Alam. “How is that the PMD’s fault? The blame lies squarely with the local administrations.”

He gives the infamous example of the New Honeymoon Hotel in Kalam which was washed away in 2010, and again in 2022. They rebuilt it each time.

Advanced radar and private analytics can pinpoint the exact minute the deluge arrives, but until district officials act on incoming alerts, enforce zoning laws, and translate data into sirens for people, the country will keep describing every climate tragedy as an inevitable “act of God” instead of one that should hold humans accountable in government.

The cost of delayed forecasts

When the sky ruptured over Buner last year, Salim Khan, a journalist, was at home in Pacha Killay. Before his eyes, the Pir Baba bazaar—the valley’s economic spine—was swallowed whole. From the third floor, Khan watched charpoys, cars, goats, dissolve. “I saw human bodies being swept away,” he says. “I was recording these scenes for my television channel, but even a journalist behind the camera is, after all, only human. I found myself unable to hold back the tears.”

On the flat roof of a submerged school, a cluster of children huddled. Roads were severed, leaving neighbours to haul the injured in their own pickup trucks. At a hospital, the death toll escalated so fast that basic supplies ran out.

“There were not enough kafans (burial shrouds),” says Khan. Announcements were made from mosques after which people began arriving at the hospital with shrouds from their own homes. Among the dead was a mother still clasping her infant to her chest, later laid to rest together in a single grave.

The survivors said they had only heard broad forecasts of seasonal rain, the kind of advisories routinely issued across bureaucratic channels, but nothing that actually explained what could happen.

The PMD’s broad-strokes are designed for regional summaries. Agile independent forecasters often spot convective spikes on satellite feeds but their apparatus does not have the integrated, hyper-localised distribution channels required to translate warnings into sirens on the ground. And till this gap is narrowed, deadly waters will continue to fill it.

item.title: Mirza Fakhrul’s real test will come in 2031. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
When the Constitution of Bangladesh was amended in 1991 and the parliamentary system was reinstated, the then interim president is said to have made an interesting observation.
Seeing that virtually all the powers of the president had been taken away by the amendment, Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed remarked: “The president will now have no other work to do except visit the shrines.”
However, it cannot be said that all presidents have been able to visit shrines peacefully.
In Bangladesh’s deeply divided political landscape, a deceased leader is sometimes feared more than a living one.
In 2002, the BNP forced its own nominated president, Badruddoza Chowdhury, to resign after only seven months in office. His crime? He had expressed a desire to visit the grave of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. Some say, however, that president Chowdhury had expressed reluctance to visit the grave of former president Ziaur Rahman, the founder of the BNP.
Whatever the truth, Badruddoza Chowdhury had to leave Bangabhaban in disgrace amid the controversy over which grave he would or would not visit.
The present is not free of controversy either.
Many had expected the new Parliament to do two things at the beginning of its session: Establish an upper house with 105 members, and then elect a new president through a vote of the members of both houses.
The debate over how members of the upper house would be elected, according to the proportion of votes received in the general election or the proportion of seats won in the lower house, ended with the BNP’s absolute victory.
Meanwhile, some significant changes to the powers of the president are also expected, if the “July Charter” is indeed a meaningful document for the BNP.
Caretaker is coming
However, even before all this, a new president was elected on August 20.
There has hardly been any adverse reaction to the person elected.
It would not be wrong to say that Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir is one of the most experienced and respected politicians not only in the BNP but also in Bangladesh.
He visited the grave of Ziaur Rahman but expressed no desire to visit the grave of Bangabandhu. He has passed the initial test of survival. But the discussion over the future of the presidency has not ended with this election, it may only have begun.
Why Awami League-nominated Md Sahabuddin remained president for six months even after the BNP secured a two-thirds majority in the election is also a matter of curiosity and deserves analysis.
There is little doubt that Mirza Fakhrul’s work as president will largely be limited to formalities. But even if the president has nothing to do for the next four and a half years except “visit the shrines,” the final six months will be eventful.
Under the current system, elections must be held within 90 days before the expiry of Parliament’s term. In other words, Parliament remains in session during the election.
But the High Court has already reinstated the system of holding elections under a non-partisan, impartial caretaker government. All that remains is to determine the process for selecting the chief adviser and other members of the caretaker government and to incorporate the necessary amendments into the Constitution.
In principle, Bangladesh’s 2031 general election will be held under a caretaker government.
Biswas to Iazuddin
A feature of the caretaker system is that the prime minister will request the president in writing to dissolve Parliament only after the existing Parliament has completed its full five-year term.
The government will also resign, and the chief adviser of the caretaker government will take the oath of office and begin work.
The president will play a major role during this period, as he will be the only elected officeholder, the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and the wheels of the bureaucracy will turn on his orders.
Here, one can look back to 2001.
Justice Latifur Rahman made 13 secretaries OSD within an hour of taking office as chief adviser on July 15.
His move created a stir in political circles. There was strong suspicion within the Awami League, the party that had just left power, that Justice Rahman would work against it.
But the fact is that the new chief adviser sidelined secretaries appointed by the Awami League in order to work impartially. He did not do this alone. He acted in consultation with the then president, Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed.
Two other instances can be recalled. First, Justice Habibur Rahman took over as chief adviser after the caretaker system was introduced in 1996. But when Army Chief General Mohammad Nasim tried to seize power, some senior officers helped President Abdur Rahman Biswas at Bangabhaban foil the coup attempt.
Second, in 2006, the ruling BNP tried to secure a chief adviser of its choice by increasing the retirement age of judges. After this attempt to manipulate the caretaker system failed, BNP-nominated President Iazuddin Ahmed declared himself chief adviser.
Many suspected at the time that President Ahmed was acting in consultation with the recently departed prime minister, Khaleda Zia. But that attempt to influence the election also failed when Iazuddin Ahmed, under pressure from the army, declared a state of emergency and postponed the election.
Md Sahabuddin’s disrespect
Against this diverse and turbulent backdrop, Mirza Fakhrul will face a test of impartiality and integrity. The country’s next election will be held within three months of the end of the 13th Parliament.
Those three months will be the most important and consequential period of Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir’s presidency.
The date of the presidential election, the 20th of this month, appears to have been carefully chosen. The respect Tarique Rahman showed President Md Sahabuddin does not appear to have been mere courtesy.
Sahabuddin once complained that the chief adviser of the interim government had shown him no respect at all and had instead humiliated him. He wanted to resign at the time. But, overwhelmed by Tarique Rahman’s respect, he remained in office.
Six months later, the BNP government forced President Md Sahabuddin to resign. There did not appear to be much respect on display then. He was not even invited to the swearing-in ceremony of the new president.
With the presidential election taking place six months after the formation of Parliament, Mirza Fakhrul’s term will expire in August 2031. That means he will remain in this crucial position throughout the entire election period under the caretaker government.
What kind of role will he play? Can he rise above his loyalty to the party and play a neutral role in the interests of the country?
Mirza Fakhrul’s answer is “yes.”
He has resigned from all BNP posts and announced that he has severed his ties with the party. He has said that he will now act impartially.
Maladaptive political culture
It is certainly reassuring to hear Mirza Fakhrul’s words, and ordinary people will hope that he can act accordingly.
But they also know how difficult it is to play a genuinely “neutral” role in Bangladesh’s bitter and vindictive political culture.
For example, it is practically impossible to deny Sheikh Mujib’s place in Bangladesh’s independence struggle and political history. But will Mirza Fakhrul be able to acknowledge this truth in any of his speeches? If he can, it will be a sign of his political wisdom and maturity -- and, perhaps more importantly, that of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
People will not expect the impossible from the president. No one will expect him to go beyond his constitutional limitations and perform some miracle.
They will simply expect the president to make it easier for his chief adviser to uphold the central principle of the caretaker government system, ensuring a free and fair election.
However, it is also true that no president has so far been able to overturn an election. Since the caretaker system was incorporated into the Constitution, three elections have been held under this arrangement.
Two were conducted under BNP-nominated presidents, and Khaleda Zia’s party was defeated in both.
The election held under an Awami League-nominated president resulted in disaster for Sheikh Hasina.
What the situation will look like in 2031, however, is difficult to predict.
Sabir Mustafa is former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: The Makkah defense pact and Bangladesh: A test of strategic autonomy. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
From the Middle East to South Asia, the strategic map is changing rapidly. Prolonged wars, regional conflicts, economic uncertainty, and intensifying rivalry among major powers are prompting states to rethink how they secure their national interests.
One of the most significant recent developments is the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, signed in Makkah on August 7, 2026 by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan. The agreement states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all three, while also calling for broader defense cooperation.
For Bangladesh, the issue is no longer merely whether it should join the Makkah framework. The larger question is how Dhaka can develop a defense and foreign-policy strategy that maximizes its security options without becoming strategically dependent on any single power or drawn into conflicts unrelated to its national interests.
Recent statements from Bangladesh indicate that Dhaka is keeping the possibility of participation open. Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir has said that Bangladesh views the possibility positively but would consider any such arrangement in light of its national interests and the changing global environment. This is not the same as a decision to join, but it makes the strategic debate increasingly relevant.
More than an “Islamic NATO”
The Makkah agreement has understandably been described in some quarters as an emerging “Islamic NATO.” Such a description, however, is premature. NATO possesses a highly developed institutional structure, integrated command arrangements, and decades of operational experience. The Makkah framework is at a much earlier stage.
Nevertheless, its political and strategic significance should not be underestimated. Saudi Arabia contributes enormous financial resources and considerable geopolitical influence; Türkiye brings a sophisticated and increasingly autonomous defense industry, NATO experience and advanced capabilities in drones, electronic warfare, and other military technologies; while Pakistan contributes a large and experienced military and nuclear capability.
The agreement therefore brings together three complementary sources of strategic power. If implemented effectively, it could eventually facilitate greater cooperation in defense production, military training, intelligence, technology transfer, and collective deterrence. Türkiye's foreign minister has also indicated that the pact is not directed against any particular country and that other states could potentially participate in the future.
Why now?
The emergence of the Makkah framework must be understood against a rapidly deteriorating regional security environment. The Israeli strike on Hamas leadership in Doha in 2025 demonstrated that even states traditionally viewed as relatively secure could find themselves exposed to the spillover effects of regional conflicts. Qatar, an important mediator between Israel and Hamas, condemned the strike as a violation of its sovereignty.
The subsequent escalation of regional tensions, including the 2026 Iran-related conflict and attacks affecting Gulf security, has reinforced the perception among regional powers that they cannot rely indefinitely on external security guarantees.
The Makkah initiative can therefore be interpreted partly as an effort to strengthen regional strategic autonomy. It does not necessarily represent a rejection of the United States or existing alliances. Rather, it reflects a broader trend in which regional powers seek greater capacity to manage their own security environment.
What could Bangladesh gain?
Bangladesh has legitimate reasons to examine the development carefully. Its defense capabilities remain significantly dependent on imported equipment and technology. Türkiye's growing defense industry could provide opportunities in drones, unmanned systems, naval platforms, electronic warfare, and defense manufacturing. Saudi Arabia offers financial strength and investment potential, while Pakistan has extensive military experience and established institutions for military education and training.
Bangladesh already maintains separate relationships with all three countries. Saudi Arabia is important to Bangladesh because of labour migration, remittances, investment, energy, and broader political and cultural ties. Türkiye is becoming an increasingly important economic and defense partner. Relations with Pakistan remain historically sensitive because of the legacy of 1971, but contemporary diplomatic, economic, educational, and military contacts have expanded.
A carefully designed engagement with the Makkah framework could therefore offer Bangladesh three potential advantages:
But these benefits must be weighed against substantial risks.
Bangladesh's security environment is different
The principal weakness of simply joining an existing security framework is that Bangladesh's security priorities are not identical to those of Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, or Pakistan.
Saudi Arabia's primary security concerns are centred on the Gulf and the wider Middle East. Pakistan's strategic calculations are deeply influenced by India, Afghanistan, and South Asian military competition. Türkiye's security environment encompasses Europe, the Black Sea, the Middle East, and its NATO commitments.
Bangladesh's priorities are different: Relations with India, the Bay of Bengal, the situation in Myanmar and Rakhine, border security, maritime trade routes, the Indian Ocean, and emerging climate-related security challenges.
Consequently, Bangladesh should not automatically adopt another country's threat perceptions as its own.
This distinction is particularly important because of the collective-defense provision. If Bangladesh were to become a formal member of a pact under which an attack on Pakistan could potentially trigger obligations toward Pakistan, India's assessment of Bangladesh's strategic orientation would inevitably change. Defense cooperation with Türkiye is one thing; participation in a collective-defense arrangement involving Pakistan is strategically much more consequential.
Managing India, China, and the United States
India would naturally watch any Bangladeshi move toward the Makkah framework closely. Bangladesh therefore needs to avoid creating the perception that its defense policy is being directed against India.
China would also have strong reasons to monitor developments. Pakistan is one of Beijing's closest strategic partners, while China maintains substantial economic and diplomatic relations with Türkiye and Saudi Arabia. Bangladesh itself is an important Chinese economic and defense partner. Greater Bangladeshi diversification of defense relationships could therefore encourage Beijing to strengthen rather than reduce its engagement with Dhaka.
Washington would view the development through the wider lens of the Indo-Pacific. Bangladesh's strategic location along the Bay of Bengal makes its foreign and defense policies relevant to maritime security and the wider Indo-Pacific balance.
This is where Bangladesh's diplomatic skill will be tested.
From weapons buyer to technology partner
The most important lesson for Bangladesh is that defense diplomacy should not be reduced to purchasing weapons.
Buying fighter aircraft from one country, drones from another, and missiles from a third may diversify suppliers, but it does not necessarily create strategic autonomy. Bangladesh could remain a permanent consumer in the global arms market.
A more ambitious objective would be to acquire technology, production capability, and knowledge.
Bangladesh should explore joint development and local production of drones and unmanned systems, military electronics, surveillance equipment, communications systems, and selected naval technologies. Cooperation with Türkiye could be particularly valuable in this regard. Defense-industrial cooperation can also stimulate research, skilled employment, technological innovation, and broader industrial development.
The strategic question should therefore change from “Where can Bangladesh buy weapons?” to “How can Bangladesh become a partner in developing and producing defense technology?”
A better option: Diversified defense diplomacy
For Bangladesh, the most realistic strategy may be diversified and issue-based defense cooperation rather than membership in a rigid military bloc.
Dhaka can deepen defense-technology cooperation with Türkiye; expand investment, training and maritime-security cooperation with Saudi Arabia; maintain selective military education, training, and peacekeeping cooperation with Pakistan; continue appropriate defense and technological cooperation with China; pursue maritime surveillance and advanced technological cooperation with the United States and European partners; and maintain pragmatic security cooperation with India on border management, maritime affairs, counterterrorism, and regional stability.
Such an approach would maximize Bangladesh's options while minimizing dependence.
Three principles should guide any future defense agreement.
First , Bangladesh should avoid joining a military alliance explicitly directed against another state.
Second , Bangladeshi territory should never become a foreign military base or a platform for military operations against another country.
Third , Bangladesh should avoid excessive dependence on any single country's weapons, technology or defense infrastructure.
A fourth principle is equally important: Before entering any major security agreement, Bangladesh must assess not only the immediate military benefits but also the economic costs, diplomatic consequences, and potential obligations that could arise during a future conflict.
Strategic autonomy, not strategic isolation
The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement could become an important new element in the security architecture of the Middle East and the wider Muslim world. Whether it remains a limited trilateral arrangement or evolves into a broader regional framework is still uncertain. What is clear, however, is that the agreement has opened a new strategic conversation.
Bangladesh should therefore watch the initiative closely rather than rush toward membership. If a formal proposal for participation emerges, Dhaka should evaluate its precise obligations, military benefits, economic costs, and diplomatic consequences before making a decision.
Bangladesh's national interest would not be served by entering an arrangement in which another country's war automatically becomes Bangladesh's war.
The country's strategic objective should instead be strategic autonomy without strategic isolation.
Bangladesh's greatest strategic asset is not a fighter aircraft, missile, or military alliance. It is geography. Situated at the intersection of South Asia and Southeast Asia and facing the Bay of Bengal, Bangladesh occupies a position of exceptional strategic importance.
If that geographical advantage is combined with effective diplomacy, economic strength, technological capacity, and credible national defense, Bangladesh can become not a follower of another country's security architecture but an influential regional actor in its own right.
The goal, therefore, should not be to choose one camp over another. It should be to build a network of partnerships in which different countries cooperate with Bangladesh in different areas, while Bangladesh retains the freedom to determine when, where, and how its national interests require engagement.
Dr Nasir Uddin Ahmed is a retired Major, researcher and political/security analyst. Email: directtoradmin2007@gmail.com .

item.title: Bangladesh, India 'very sincere' over delayed cricket series: BCB president. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh and India are “sincere” in their search for a new date for a white-ball series that was first supposed to take place last year, Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) President Tamim Iqbal said.

The three one-day internationals (ODIs) and three T20 matches in Bangladesh were originally planned for August 2025, but then political relations soured between the two countries.

The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) then said the series would be played this September, but there is no sign of it happening imminently.

“Both boards are very sincere that this thing happens,” Tamim said on the podcast Not out Noman on Sunday.

“Both BCCI and BCB, we are looking at windows as well, which time what can be done.”

He added, “Intentions are very positive.”

There was no immediate response from the BCCI.

Dhaka and New Delhi have been at odds since a 2024 mass uprising toppled then-Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina.

She fled to India, her long-time ally, where she remains in hiding.

In February, Bangladesh refused to send a team to India for the T20 World Cup, citing security concerns.

India last toured Bangladesh for a cricket series in 2022. Bangladesh visited India in September-October 2024.

item.description:
The planned $550 million Laldia Terminal is one of the most ambitious port projects Bangladesh has taken on - one that has the potential to reshape Chittagong.
A modern terminal with expanded capacity, efficient cargo handling, and improved connectivity is exactly what we need to keep pace with rising export volumes and global shipping demands. Above all else, this is what we need as Bangladesh looks to take the meaningful next step in its development journey.
Done right, this could become a cornerstone of Bangladesh’s economic future, but ambition alone is not enough. We have seen too many large infrastructure projects suffer from delays, cost overruns, and coordination failures. The Laldia Terminal cannot afford to join that list.
Given that the port is projected to be made entirely with foreign investment, there is an even greater need to ensure this is done right. Foreign investment continues to be a challenge for our nation, and ensuring the port development stays on track is one way to instil confidence into future investors.
As such, this project must be executed with discipline: Strict adherence to timelines, transparent procurement, and rigorous oversight.
Moreover, future development for Bangladesh must be built upon the principles of sustainability, with a clear operational plan that ensures projects deliver the benefits promised.
If implemented properly, the terminal will strengthen Bangladesh’s position in global supply chains, support export‑led growth, and ease the strain on existing port facilities. It is a project that can genuinely transform Chittagong -- but only if it is treated with the urgency it deserves and not yet another slow‑moving development scheme.
Bangladesh needs this terminal. Now it must prove it can deliver it -- on time, on budget, and with the seriousness our future demands.

item.title: Promises on e‑rickshaw regulation mean nothing without action. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The government moving to bring e-rickshaws under a policy framework, with systematic licensing and registration planned through local government, is unquestionably a positive development - on paper.
However, Bangladesh has heard this promise before.
For some time now, authorities have announced plans to register, regulate, and reorganize these vehicles, only for the initiatives to stall, fade, or be quietly abandoned.
This time, the country needs more than statements. It needs implementation.
E‑rickshaws are now an essential part of Bangladesh’s transport ecosystem and play a significant role in providing affordable mobility in addition to creating livelihoods for hundreds of thousands. None of this has ever been disputed.
Yet, their rapid, unregulated growth coupled with their high-risk has also created serious problems. Untrained drivers should never have been allowed to operate these vehicles, and it is no wonder that Dhaka has seen increased traffic chaos and more frequent accidents.
Without proper oversight, a mode of transport that should help communities has unfortunately ended up putting them at risk, not to mention worsen our traffic woes.
The government’s renewed commitment to registration, route management, and safety standards is therefore welcome - but credibility depends entirely on follow‑through.
We expect the government to realize why past attempts failed and not give in to coercion from vested interests resisting change. Unless these structural issues are addressed, this latest initiative will meet the same fate.
Bangladesh cannot afford another cycle of announcements without action. E‑rickshaws are here to stay and the goal now is to transform them from the source of disorder they are today to becoming a safe, integrated part of the transport system.
